sentences.text: The great auk belongs to the genus Pinguinus, which contained only this single modern species.
The name Pinguinus derives from the Latin word pinguis, meaning 'plump', reflecting the bird's robust build.
Adult individuals stood approximately 75 cm tall and weighed around 5 kg.
Their eggs were ovate and elongate, measuring an average of 12.4 cm in length and 7.6 cm in width.
Among the surviving skins, almost all display summer plumage, with only two belonging to immature birds.
The great auk is the only British bird known to have gone extinct in historic times.
Evidence suggests Neanderthals used these birds as a food source over 100,000 years ago, indicated by cleaned bones found near campfires.
Images believed to depict great auks were carved into cave walls in Spain and Italy more than 35,000 years ago.
A specimen purchased in 1971 for £9000 holds the Guinness Book of Records title for the most expensive stuffed bird ever sold.
The current locations of six great auk eggs remain unknown.
The species was officially declared extinct in 1852.
Charles d'Ecluse first described the bird as Mergus Americanus in 1605.
It received its first official legal protection in 1553.
Carl Linnaeus formally described the great auk in 1758.
The bird primarily fed on fish such as Atlantic menhaden and capelin, as well as crustaceans.
It was an excellent swimmer that used its wings to propel itself underwater.
The great auk could hold its breath for 15 minutes, a duration longer than that of a seal.
Its main diet consisted of fish generally 12 to 20 cm in length and weighing 40 to 50 g.
Remains from Funk Island suggest Atlantic menhaden and capelin were the great auk's favored prey.
Great auks began their breeding pairing season in early to mid-May.
These birds formed lifelong mating pairs.
To establish nesting colonies, they required rocky islands with gently sloping coastlines that facilitated access to the sea.

The great auk was never observed or described by modern scientists during its existence; it is known only through accounts from non-experts like sailors, making its behavior poorly documented and difficult to reconstruct.
Although it occasionally caught prey reaching up to half its own body length, its main diet consisted of fish, generally 12 to 20 cm in length and weighing 40 to 50 g.
The great auk was closely related to the little auk or dovekie.
Some ornithologists still argue that the great auk should remain in the genus Alca.
Fossil evidence of the great auk dates from the Middle Pleistocene to the Holocene.
The species first appeared around 400,000 years ago.
The oldest fossils of the modern great auk come from Boxgrove in England and Lower Town Hill in Bermuda, dating to at least 400,000 years ago.
Some researchers consider a 1852 report to be the last sighting of a great auk.
After Pinguinus alfrednewtoni went extinct, the great auk expanded into its former territory.
